hints: Think about which acid acts as the acid and which acts as the base when concentrated nitric and sulfuric acids mix, and what small molecule is lost to leave $\text{NO}_2^+$.
walkthrough:
See sulfuric acid as the stronger acid**
Picture concentrated sulfuric acid protonating nitric acid. Nitric acid accepts a proton to become $\text{H}_2\text{NO}_3^+$, which then loses water to leave the linear electrophile $\text{NO}_2^+$. The sulfuric acid becomes $\text{HSO}_4^-$.
Final answer: $\text{HNO}_3 + \text{H}_2\text{SO}_4 \rightarrow \text{NO}_2^+ + \text{HSO}_4^- + \text{H}_2\text{O}$

hints: Recall where the pair of electrons that attacks the electrophile comes from in electrophilic substitution.
Think about what the ring looks like once aromaticity is temporarily broken and where the positive charge sits.
Consider which bond breaks to restore aromaticity and what small ion is expelled alongside the nitro product.
walkthrough:
Attack by the ring**
Keep in mind the benzene $\pi$ cloud is the nucleophile. Draw a curly arrow starting inside the hexagon and pointing to the N atom of $\text{NO}_2^+$. The N-O bonds stay intact, the N gains the new C-N bond.

Draw the intermediate correctly**
Once the new bond forms, aromaticity is lost. Show the cyclohexadienyl cation (arenium ion) with the $\text{NO}_2$ group attached ortho to $\text{CH}_3$, a broken ring with one double bond pattern changed, and the + charge delocalised over the remaining $\pi$ system. A common slip is to put the + on the carbon bearing $\text{NO}_2$, keep it delocalised.

Restore aromaticity**
Now a base removes the hydrogen from the same carbon that was attacked. Draw a curly arrow from that C-H bond back into the ring to reform the $\pi$ system, and show $\text{H}^+$ as the second product alongside 1-methyl-2-nitrobenzene.

Final answer: Curly arrow from benzene $\pi$ system to N of $\text{NO}_2^+$; arenium ion intermediate with $\text{NO}_2$ attached at 2-position to $\text{CH}_3$ and + charge delocalised in ring; curly arrow from C-H bond at that carbon back into ring to reform aromaticity + $\text{H}^+$.

hints: Focus on the oxygen atom in phenol and what its lone pair can do with the benzene $\pi$ system.
Link increased electron density in the ring to how easily it attracts a positive electrophile like $\text{NO}_2^+$.
walkthrough:
Spot the donation**
Look at the -OH group. Oxygen has lone pairs in a p-orbital that can overlap sideways with the benzene $\pi$ system. That means electron density is pushed from oxygen into the ring.

Connect to reactivity**
A more electron rich ring is a stronger nucleophile. It attracts $\text{NO}_2^+$ more strongly and the activation energy for forming the arenium ion is lower. So dilute $\text{HNO}_3$ alone is enough, no need for concentrated $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ to make a high concentration of $\text{NO}_2^+$.

Final answer: Lone pair / p-orbital on O delocalises / overlaps into the ring $\pi$ system; this increases electron density of the ring so it is more readily attacked / polarises $\text{NO}_2^+$ more easily, hence milder conditions.

hints: Remember phenols are acidic enough to react with Na metal like alcohols do, forming an O-Na salt and a familiar gas.
walkthrough:
Treat it as an acid plus metal**
The phenolic O-H behaves as a weak acid. Sodium removes the phenolic H to give the ionic $\text{O}^-\text{Na}^+$ group, while $\text{H}$ atoms combine to $\text{H}_2$. The $\text{NO}_2$ group is unchanged. Balance as two phenols to one hydrogen molecule.
Final answer: 2-$\text{O}^-\text{Na}^+$ nitrophenolate (sodium 2-nitrophenolate) + $\text{H}_2$; i.e. $2\text{ArOH} + 2\text{Na} \rightarrow 2\text{ArONa} + \text{H}_2$

hints: Identify the change $\text{NO}_2$ to $\text{NH}_2$ as a gain of electrons and recall the classic hot metal plus acid pair for nitroarenes.
walkthrough:
Name the reducing system**
Changing $\text{NO}_2$ to $\text{NH}_2$ needs 6 electrons. The standard laboratory method is heating with tin metal and concentrated hydrochloric acid. Do not write just $\text{H}_2$/Ni or $\text{NaBH}_4$, they are not the required reagent for this reduction.
Final answer: Hot Sn / tin with concentrated $\text{HCl}$ (followed by alkali to liberate free amine).

hints: Check whether oxygen is lost or hydrogen is gained when $\text{NO}_2$ becomes $\text{NH}_2$.
walkthrough:
Classify by oxygen loss**
$\text{NO}_2$ loses oxygen and gains hydrogen to become $\text{NH}_2$. Loss of oxygen or gain of electrons is reduction.
Final answer: Reduction

hints: Think about which group in 2-nitrophenol attacks $\text{CH}_3\text{COCl}$ and what $\text{OCOCH}_3$ ester linkage replaces.
walkthrough:
Form the ester**
The phenolic OH attacks the carbonyl carbon of ethanoyl chloride. HCl is lost and the OH becomes $\text{OCOCH}_3$. Keep the $\text{NO}_2$ ortho to it. The product is the phenyl ester, not a carboxylic acid.
Final answer: Benzene ring with $\text{OCOCH}_3$ and $\text{NO}_2$ in 1,2-positions (2-nitrophenyl ethanoate).

hints: Recall the two stage mechanism name common to all acyl chloride reactions with O- and N-nucleophiles.
walkthrough:
Name the acylation mechanism**
Attack at the C=O followed by loss of $\text{Cl}^-$ is always nucleophilic addition-elimination. Addition to form the tetrahedral intermediate, then elimination of HCl.
Final answer: (Nucleophilic) addition-elimination

hints: Start by ordering the four compounds from strongest to weakest acid, remembering nitro-phenols are stronger than phenol, which is stronger than water and alcohols.
Link stronger acidity to a weaker O-H bond and a more stable anion that loses $\text{H}^+$ more easily.
Think about how the oxygen lone pair in phenol and nitrophenol interacts with the ring compared with water and ethanol.
Consider how the alkyl group in ethanol pushes electrons toward oxygen and destabilises the ethoxide ion.
walkthrough:
State the order**
Acidity falls as: 2-nitrophenol (most acidic) > phenol > water > ethanol (least acidic). Phenols beat water and alcohols, and the electron withdrawing $\text{NO}_2$ makes nitrophenol beat phenol.

Use anion stability as the key**
Acidity is about how easily $\text{H}^+$ is donated, which depends on how stable the left behind negative ion is. A more stable anion means a weaker O-H bond and easier proton loss.

Explain phenols versus water**
In phenol and 2-nitrophenol the lone pair on O overlaps and delocalises into the ring $\pi$ system. This withdraws electron density from O, weakens O-H, and stabilises the phenoxide anion by spreading the negative charge. In 2-nitrophenol the $\text{NO}_2$ group withdraws further, stabilising even more.

Explain ethanol as weakest**
In ethanol the alkyl group is electron donating by positive inductive effect. It pushes electrons onto O, intensifies the negative charge on $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{O}^-$ and destabilises it, so ethanol holds onto its $\text{H}^+$ most strongly, even less acidic than water.

Final answer: 2-nitrophenol > phenol > water > ethanol (most to least acidic). Phenols are more acidic because anion is stabilised / O-H bond weakened so $\text{H}^+$ more easily lost; lone pair / p-orbital on O delocalises into ring; ethanol anion destabilised by positive inductive / electron donating alkyl group.

hints: Look beyond the phenol group and list the other O-containing and N-containing groups, noting how many carbons attach to the C-OH carbons and to N.
Remember primary means the functional carbon or nitrogen is attached to only one other carbon, secondary means attached to two carbons.
walkthrough:
Pick out the three groups**
Ignoring the phenol OH, salbutamol has $\text{HOCH}_2$- attached to the ring, a $\text{CH(OH)}$ in the side chain, and an $\text{NH}$ linking $\text{CH}_2$ to $\text{C(CH}_3)_3$.

Classify each**
$\text{HOCH}_2$- carbon is bonded to one carbon, so primary alcohol. $\text{CH(OH)}$ carbon is bonded to two carbons (ring side and $\text{CH}_2$), so secondary alcohol. The N is bonded to two carbons ($\text{CH}_2$ and the tert-butyl C), with one H, so secondary amine.
Final answer: Alcohol / hydroxyl: primary ($\text{HOCH}_2$-); alcohol / hydroxyl: secondary ($\text{CH(OH)}$ side chain); amine: secondary ($\text{NH}$ attached to two carbons).

hints: Remember $\text{Br}_2$(aq) substitutes H atoms ortho or para to a phenol OH, but check which positions are already blocked in salbutamol.
walkthrough:
Brominate the activated ring**
The phenol ring is so activated that $\text{Br}_2$(aq) reacts without catalyst. Bromine replaces available H ortho to the phenolic OH. All alcohol and amine side chains stay unchanged. Draw the same skeleton with Br added on the ring.
Final answer: Salbutamol ring with Br substituted ortho/para to phenolic OH (one Br atom on ring, side chains $\text{HOCH}_2$, HO, $\text{CH(OH)CH}_2\text{NHC(CH}_3)_3$ unchanged).

hints: Recall $\text{SOCl}_2$ replaces alcoholic OH with Cl but leaves phenolic OH unchanged, and use the formula $\text{C}_{13}\text{H}_{19}\text{Cl}_2\text{NO}$ to confirm how many OH groups react.
walkthrough:
Replace only alcoholic OH groups**
Excess $\text{SOCl}_2$ converts each alcohol OH into Cl with loss of $\text{SO}_2$ and HCl. Phenols do not react under these conditions, so the phenolic OH stays. That gives two Cl atoms in place of two alcoholic O atoms, matching $\text{C}_{13}\text{H}_{19}\text{Cl}_2\text{NO}$ with one O left. Draw $\text{ClCH}_2$- on the ring and $\text{CH(Cl)}$ in the side chain.

Final answer: Salbutamol skeleton with phenolic HO retained, $\text{HOCH}_2$ to $\text{ClCH}_2$ and $\text{CH(OH)}$ to $\text{CH(Cl)}$, i.e. ring with $\text{ClCH}_2$, HO and side chain $\text{CH(Cl)CH}_2\text{NHC(CH}_3)_3$.
